claims.claim: A pocket veto is a presidential power that is not subject to the congressional override process
claims.sourceSpan: Pocket vetoes are not subject to the congressional veto override process.

claims.claim: A pocket veto occurs when the President neither signs nor vetoes a bill and Congress adjourns before the 10-day period expires
claims.sourceSpan: Pocket vetoes occur when the President receives a bill but is unable to reject and return the bill to an adjourned Congress within the 10-day period.

claims.claim: Which adjournments produce a pocket veto is still disputed
claims.sourceSpan: Recent Presidents and Congresses disagree about what constitutes a pocket veto.

claims.claim: The 1987 mootness case is named: Burke v. Barnes, 479 U.S. 361 (1987)
claims.sourceSpan: Burke v. Barnes, 479 U.S. 361 (1987).

claims.claim: ADDED: the 1974 pre-election adjournment ran October 17 to November 18
claims.sourceSpan: In 1974, Congress adjourned from October 17 to November 18 for the elections.

claims.claim: ADDED: Ford claimed five pocket vetoes in that period but returned the bills to Congress anyway
claims.sourceSpan: During that intrasession period, President Gerald Ford exercised the pocket veto five times, but in a unique manner. Although he claimed to pocket veto the bills, he also returned them to Congress

claims.claim: ADDED, and the concrete answer to the page title: Congress treated those claimed pocket vetoes as return vetoes and both Houses overrode one of them, the Vocational Rehabilitation Act Amendments, on November 20 and 21; the Administration still refused to promulgate it
claims.sourceSpan: Congress treated the “pocket vetoes” as return vetoes, capable of being overridden by a two-thirds vote of each chamber. In fact, both Houses overrode the veto of the Vocational Rehabilitation Act Amendments: the House on November 20 and the Senate on November 21. Nevertheless, the Administration refused to promulgate it as a law.

claims.claim: Which adjournments produce a pocket veto is still disputed (og description; the unbounded "the courts have never settled" claim it replaced rested on a 2001 report and was removed)
claims.sourceSpan: Recent Presidents and Congresses disagree about what constitutes a pocket veto.

claims.claim: Which adjournments produce a pocket veto has been contested since 1929 and is still disputed
claims.sourceSpan: Pocket vetoes occur when the President receives a bill but is unable to reject and return the bill to an adjourned Congress within the 10-day period. The bill, though lacking a signature and formal objections, does not become law.

claims.claim: A regular veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote in each chamber
claims.sourceSpan: Passage by a two-thirds margin in both chambers is required to override a veto

claims.claim: CRS: pocket vetoes "are not subject to the congressional veto override process"
claims.sourceSpan: Pocket vetoes are not subject to the congressional veto override process.

claims.claim: Which adjournments produce a pocket veto has been contested since 1929 and is not settled
claims.sourceSpan: Beginning in 1929, several judicial decisions attempted to clarify when an adjournment by Congress would “prevent” the President from returning a veto.

claims.claim: The Article I, Section 7 pocket-veto clause, quoted verbatim
claims.sourceSpan: If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.
claims.section: Art. I, sec. 7, par. 2, quoted in the opinion

claims.claim: CRS reads that clause as the source of the regular-veto / pocket-veto distinction
claims.sourceSpan: This language allows for a distinction between “regular vetoes” (returned to Congress for an override vote) and “pocket vetoes” (not returned).

claims.claim: The only route around a pocket veto is to reintroduce and re-pass the bill
claims.sourceSpan: the only way for Congress to circumvent the pocket veto is to reintroduce the legislation as a new bill, pass it through both chambers, and present it to the President again for signature

claims.claim: A pocket veto is possible only when Congress adjourns within the 10-day window that starts at presentment
claims.sourceSpan: If, on the other hand, Congress has adjourned within the 10-day period after presentation of the bill to the President (thereby preventing the return of the bill to Congress), the President may refuse to sign the bill, and the bill does not become law

claims.claim: If Congress stays in session the President must sign, return with objections, or let it become law unsigned
claims.sourceSpan: The President may sign a bill into law within the 10-day period (excluding Sundays), let the bill become law without signature,

claims.claim: OLC (1990): a pocket veto "is not a power of the President that he exercises affirmatively"; pocket vetoes "happen automatically on the tenth day after presentment if the President has not signed the bill"
claims.sourceSpan: is not a power of the President that he exercises affirmatively. Rather, pocket vetoes happen automatically on the tenth day after presentment if the President has not signed the bill.

claims.claim: OLC: the pocket veto operates "only if the tenth day after presentment falls during an adjournment", which puts presentment scheduling in Congress's hands
claims.sourceSpan: only if the tenth day after presentment falls during an adjournment

claims.claim: OLC drew the scheduling consequence explicitly
claims.sourceSpan: the Court’s reading of the Adjournment Clause requires, at most, attention to the scheduling of presentments, so that the tenth day after presentment does not fall during an adjournment of either House that is longer than three days

claims.claim: The 1929 bill reached Coolidge on June 24, 1926, under 10 days before the July 3 adjournment ending the 69th Congress's first session
claims.sourceSpan: The bill that was litigated reached President Calvin Coolidge on June 24, 1926, less than 10 days before Congress adjourned on July 3, at the end of the first session of the 69th Congress.

claims.claim: The intersession adjournment ran until December 6, "or over five months"
claims.sourceSpan: The intersession adjournment lasted until December 6, or over five months.

claims.claim: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the pocket veto
claims.sourceSpan: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the pocket veto, concluding that the adjournment prevented the President from returning the bill.

claims.claim: The Court did NOT hold that intersession adjournments as such trigger the pocket veto; its stated test is whether the adjournment "prevents" return
claims.sourceSpan: the determinative question in reference to an 'adjournment' is not whether it is a final adjournment of Congress or an interim adjournment, such as an adjournment of the first session, but whether it is one that 'prevents' the President from returning the bill to the House in which it originated within the time allowed

claims.claim: The Court's statement that delivery to a legislative agent would not suffice was dicta
claims.sourceSpan: This latter point, regarding legislative agents, was dicta and not the central holding of the case.

claims.claim: Rehnquist, as head of OLC, endorsed that reading at Senate hearings in 1971
claims.sourceSpan: At Senate hearings in 1971, William H. Rehnquist testified as the head of the Office of Legal Counsel in the Justice Department.

claims.claim: In Wright the Senate alone recessed for three days and the bill was returned to the Secretary of the Senate
claims.sourceSpan: On Monday, May 4, 1936, the Senate took a recess until noon, Thursday, May 7, 1936. The House of Representatives remained in session. On May 5, 1936, the President returned the bill with a message addressed to the Senate setting forth his objections. The bill and message were delivered to the Secretary of the Senate.

claims.claim: Wright: "The Congress" means both Houses; the Senate alone is not "the Congress"
claims.sourceSpan: 'The Congress' did not adjourn. The Senate alone was in recess. The Constitution creates and defines 'the Congress.' It consists 'of a Senate and House of Representatives.' Article 1, § 1. The Senate is not 'the Congress.'

claims.claim: Wright: the Constitution "does not define what shall constitute a return of a bill or deny the use of appropriate agencies in effecting the return"
claims.sourceSpan: The Constitution does not define what shall constitute a return of a bill or deny the use of appropriate agencies in effecting the return.

claims.claim: Wright: "why may it not be received by the accredited agent of the legislative body?"
claims.sourceSpan: why may it not be received by the accredited agent of the legislative body?

claims.claim: Wright's holding, quoted in full with its conditions
claims.sourceSpan: We hold that where the Congress has not adjourned and the House in which the bill originated is in recess for not more than three days under the constitutional permission while Congress is in session, the bill does not become a law if the President has delivered the bill with his objections to the appropriate officer of the House within the prescribed ten days, and the Congress does not pass the bill over his objections by the requisite votes.

claims.claim: Wright expressly declined to treat the 1929 case as controlling
claims.sourceSpan: We do not regard that decision as applicable for two reasons: (1) The present question was not involved; and (2) the reasoning of the decision is inapposite to the circumstances of this case.

claims.claim: Nixon pocket vetoed the Family Practice of Medicine Bill on December 24, 1970
claims.sourceSpan: There were no further legal disputes until President Richard Nixon, on December 24, 1970, exercised a pocket veto over the Family Practice of Medicine Bill.

claims.claim: The Senate was absent four days and the House five over that Christmas break
claims.sourceSpan: Not counting December 27 (a Sunday), the Senate was absent for four days and the House for five.

claims.claim: Kennedy v. Sampson, 511 F.2d 430 (D.C. Cir. 1974): an intrasession adjournment does not prevent return "so long as appropriate arrangements are made for the receipt of presidential vetoes during the adjournment"
claims.sourceSpan: The D.C. Circuit ruled that an intrasession adjournment of Congress “does not prevent the President from returning a bill which he disapproves so long as appropriate arrangements are made for the receipt of presidential vetoes during the adjournment.”

claims.claim: The reporter citation for Kennedy v. Sampson is 511 F.2d 430 (D.C. Cir. 1974)
claims.sourceSpan: Kennedy v. Sampson, 511 F.2d 430, 437 (D.C. Cir. 1974).

claims.claim: Justice did not appeal, and the bill was printed as a public law backdated to December 25, 1970
claims.sourceSpan: The bill was eventually printed as a public law (P.L. 91-696) and backdated to December 25, 1970

claims.claim: On November 30, 1983 Reagan pocket vetoed a bill "to require certification of human rights practices in El Salvador as a precondition for sending military aid"
claims.sourceSpan: On November 30, 1983, he pocket vetoed a bill to require certification of human rights practices in El Salvador as a precondition for sending military aid.

claims.claim: The intersession adjournment ran nine weeks (House adjourned sine die November 18, returned January 23, 1984)
claims.sourceSpan: The House had adjourned sine die on November 18 and did not return until January 23, 1984––nine weeks later.

claims.claim: A district court upheld Reagan, following the 1929 case
claims.sourceSpan: A district court upheld President Reagan’s action. The judge reasoned that the case most pertinent was the Pocket Veto Case of 1929

claims.claim: The D.C. Circuit reversed in Barnes v. Kline, 759 F.2d 21 (1985)
claims.sourceSpan: Barnes v. Kline, 759 F.2d 21, 30 (D.C. Cir. 1985).

claims.claim: The D.C. Circuit reasoned that Congress had appointed agents and so had facilitated, not prevented, return
claims.sourceSpan: It is difficult to understand how Congress could be said to have prevented return of H.R. 4042 simply by adjourning. Rather, by appointing agents for receipt of veto messages, Congress affirmatively facilitated return of the bill in the eventuality that the President would disapprove it.

claims.claim: In 1987 the Supreme Court held the controversy moot because the bill had expired by its own terms
claims.sourceSpan: in 1987 the Supreme Court held that the controversy over the El Salvador legislation was moot because the bill had expired by its own terms, regardless of whether it had been previously enacted into law or not

claims.claim: CRS: judicial interpretations remain unclear because the Court sidestepped on mootness
claims.sourceSpan: judicial interpretations of the pocket veto power remain unclear because the Supreme Court in 1987 decided to sidestep a pocket veto issue on procedural grounds (mootness) rather than reach a substantive holding

claims.claim: CRS describes a Ford/Carter accommodation limiting the pocket veto to sine die adjournment at the end of the second session, provided Congress had instructed agents
claims.sourceSpan: limiting the pocket veto to the end of the second session of a Congress, after Congress had adjourned sine die, provided that Congress has instructed legislative agents to receive presidential messages

claims.claim: All 18 of Carter's pocket vetoes came after a sine die adjournment
claims.sourceSpan: All of his 18 pocket vetoes were exercised after Congress had adjourned sine die at the end of the second sessions of the 95th and 96th Congresses.

claims.claim: That accommodation was disrupted by Reagan, Bush and Clinton
claims.sourceSpan: has been disrupted in the past three administrations of Presidents Reagan, Bush, and Clinton, who invoked the pocket veto between the first and second sessions and at times in the middle of a session

claims.claim: The "protective return" is a hybrid the Justice Department names: the President claims the pocket veto and returns the bill anyway
claims.sourceSpan: A “protective return” is a hybrid: the President claims the power of pocket veto but, at the same time, returns the bill to Congress for a possible override.

claims.claim: CRS conclusion: the status of these pocket vetoes remains unclear, and Congress has taken override votes on them
claims.sourceSpan: The status of these “pocket vetoes” remains unclear because Presidents claim the pocket veto power while at the same time they return the bill to Congress for a possible override. In a number of cases, Congress has taken votes in an effort to override these vetoes.

claims.claim: Efforts to define "adjournment" by statute had not succeeded as of the March 2001 report, which is how the page now states it

claims.claim: REMOVED: "The Supreme Court's 1929 decision in The Pocket Veto Case (279 U.S. 655) held that an adjournment between sessions does trigger pocket veto availability." The Court said in terms that the intersession/final distinction is NOT the test - "the determinative question ... is not whether it is a final adjournment of Congress or an interim adjournment ... but whether it is one that 'prevents' the President from returning the bill". The article stated as the holding the very proposition the opinion disclaimed. Replaced with the case's facts, its result, and its own test.

REMOVED: "Courts have been divided on this," supported by naming the 1929 case and Kennedy v. Sampson. Those two do not conflict - they address different adjournments, and Wright expressly distinguishes the 1929 case rather than disagreeing with it. The real division (Barnes v. Carmen upheld, Barnes v. Kline reversed, Burke v. Barnes mooted) was absent from the page and is now the paragraph that carries the point.

REMOVED: "Congress now routinely leaves officers available to receive presidential communications during recesses specifically to limit the window for pocket vetoes." Neither "routinely" nor the attributed motive is in any stored source; RL30909 describes SPECIFIC arrangements in specific years and then says Congress "could take other actions to protect its prerogatives during a recess or adjournment" - the language of an option, not a routine. First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, Phase B session 7 (veto cluster), run against the same stored source set as presidential-veto plus CRS RL30909 and two Supreme Court opinions.

THE SWEEP'S WORST FINDING IS PARTLY REJECTED AND A DIFFERENT ONE PUT IN ITS PLACE. Phase A graded the Kennedy v. Sampson sentence an F-FAIL because Wright v. United States supposedly CONTRADICTS the 'appointed an agent' condition. It does not: Wright concerns a three-day recess of one chamber and holds that the Senate alone is not 'the Congress', and RL30909 paraphrases Kennedy v. Sampson's condition in almost the article's own words. The sweep's real point - that Wright is the controlling Supreme Court authority sitting between the two cases the article named, and was never cited - is upheld, and Wright is now quoted at length including its full holding with every condition attached.

THE ACTUAL WORST DEFECT WAS ON NOBODY'S LIST. The article stated as the 1929 holding the very proposition that opinion disclaims. It said The Pocket Veto Case 'held that an adjournment between sessions does trigger pocket veto availability'; the Court said 'the determinative question in reference to an adjournment is not whether it is a final adjournment of Congress or an interim adjournment, such as an adjournment of the first session, but whether it is one that prevents the President from returning the bill to the House in which it originated within the time allowed'. The article also told readers 'Courts have been divided on this' and then named two cases that are not in conflict, while omitting the division that actually happened - Barnes v. Carmen upheld, Barnes v. Kline reversed, and the Supreme Court disposing of Burke v. Barnes on mootness in 1987 rather than deciding it.

AND IT PRESENTED AN UNSETTLED AREA AS SETTLED. Nothing on the page told readers that the Ford/Carter accommodation broke down, that presidents since have claimed pocket vetoes intersession and mid-session, that the Justice Department's 'protective return' means a claimed pocket veto is often returned to Congress anyway, or that Congress has taken override votes on them. All of that is now on the page, bounded to RL30909's March 2001 edition, and the meta and og descriptions were rewritten to stop asserting a settled rule. The title still says 'The Presidential Power That Can't Be Overridden' - sourced to RS22188, but flagged for James, because retitling an indexed page is an SEO call.

REMOVED, not softened: 'Congress now routinely leaves officers available ... specifically to limit the window for pocket vetoes' (neither the routine nor the motive is in any source; RL30909 says Congress COULD take such steps); 'The most common opportunity for a pocket veto is end-of-session legislation' (no source ranks scenarios); 'physically cannot receive the returned bill' (the test is 'prevents', and Wright upheld a return to a chamber that was not sitting); 'delivered to the White House by the Congress' ('White House' appears in Wright only inside an analogy).

VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the sweep flagged 'Franklin Roosevelt used pocket vetoes more than any other president' as an unchecked superlative.
